title: One Codebase or Many
summary: Brightbasket, a grocery-delivery startup, outgrows its single app. When should one codebase become many services, and what does the split cost?

goals.text: Name what a monolith couples: deploys, failures and data
Split safely with a modular monolith and the strangler fig
Count the network and data costs of microservices
Choose an architecture from your team shape

steps.title: Everything in one box
body: Brightbasket delivers groceries in three cities. The whole product — catalog, cart, payments, recommendations — is one codebase, built into one artifact and deployed as one process. That's a monolith.

For a team of six, it's the right call: one repo to search, one thing to deploy, one database where any feature can JOIN any table, and calls between features are plain function calls that cost nanoseconds.

steps.title: Sixty people, one release
body: Two years later there are eight teams and sixty engineers, all merging into the same artifact. A change to the cart can't ship until everyone else's changes are tested together, so releases batch up into a weekly release train.
This is deploy coupling: unrelated work shares one pipeline, one test suite and one rollout. Bigger batches mean riskier releases, which means more caution, which means even bigger batches.
changes: + 8 teams merging into one codebase
+ Queue of changes waiting for the release train

steps.title: One bug, whole site
body: Tuesday's train carries a memory leak in the recommendations widget — a nice-to-have feature. The leak grows until the process is killed, and because everything shares one process, checkout dies with it.
The monolith also couples blast radius and scaling: you can't give recommendations more memory, or run payments on more machines, without scaling every feature together.

callout.text: In one process, the least important code can take down the most important code.

changes: ~ Monolith overloaded by a leak in one module
~ Load balancer returns 502s

steps.title: Draw the seams first
body: Before reaching for the network, Brightbasket splits the code inside the monolith: a modular monolith. Each module owns its own tables and exposes a small public interface; nothing reaches into another module's internals or schema.

Teams can now work in parallel with far fewer collisions, and the boundaries are cheap to move while you're still learning where they belong. It's still one deploy, though — so blast radius hasn't changed yet.

callout.text: If you can't keep modules apart inside one process, separate services will just become a distributed mess.

changes: ~ Monolith split into Catalog, Cart and Payments modules
~ One schema per module
- Cross-module table access

steps.title: Carve off one piece
body: Rewriting everything at once is how migrations die. Instead they use the strangler fig pattern: put a router in front, build one new service beside the old app, and send just its traffic there.

Recommendations go first — they're low-risk and were the ones leaking memory. If the new service misbehaves, the router flips /recs back. Piece by piece, the monolith shrinks until nothing is left to route to it.
changes: + Edge router sends /recs to the new service
+ Recs service with its own store
~ Monolith no longer serves recommendations

steps.title: Many small deployables
body: A year on, each area is its own microservice: its own repo, pipeline, deploy schedule and database. An API gateway hides the split from the apps.
Each team ships when it's ready — dozens of deploys a day — and a crash in Recs now takes down one feature, not the store. Payments can run on twenty instances while Recs runs on three.
changes: + Catalog, Cart, Payments and Recs services
+ A database per service
~ Load balancer is now an API gateway
- Monolith retired

steps.title: Function calls became network calls
body: The cart page used to make in-process calls to get prices and payment limits. Now each is a network hop with serialization, timeouts and retries — thousands of times slower, and any hop can fail.

Chains of calls multiply tail latency: if each of six calls has a 1% chance of being slow, about 6% of page loads hit at least one slow call. Every new service needs timeouts, retries with backoff and tracing just to stay as reliable as the monolith was for free.

callout.text: Avoid chatty chains: design service APIs so one page needs a few coarse calls, not many tiny ones.

changes: + Cart calls Catalog and Payments per request
~ Cart → Catalog drops some calls

card.title: The network tax
lines: # one page view, before vs after the split
! every hop can be slow, or fail

steps.title: No more JOINs across the line
body: With data ownership, only Catalog may touch the products table. Cart can't simply JOIN to it any more; reaching into another service's database would re-couple everything you just separated.

Instead Cart asks Catalog's API, or keeps its own copy of the few fields it needs, updated from events like PriceChanged. That copy is briefly stale — you've traded one transaction across everything for eventual consistency between services.
changes: + Catalog publishes PriceChanged events
+ Cart keeps a local copy of prices
- Direct reads of another service's tables

steps.title: Architecture follows the org chart
body: Services mostly solve a people problem: letting many teams ship independently. Systems end up mirroring the communication structure of the teams that build them, so draw service lines where team lines are.

A five-person startup with ten microservices pays the full operational bill — deploy pipelines, observability, on-call for each — without the benefit. Start modular, split when deploy queues and blast radius actually hurt.
changes: ~ Each service owned by exactly one team

steps.title: One codebase or many: recap
body:
• Monolith → simple and fast, but deploys, failures and scaling are coupled
  • Modular monolith → clean seams and owned schemas, still one deploy
  • Strangler fig → migrate one route at a time behind a router
  • Microservices → independent deploys and small blast radius
  • The bill → network hops, no cross-service JOINs, much more to operate
